# Screen Time, Sleep, and a Brief Sleep-Hygiene Intervention in Adolescents

## Introduction

In recent years, adolescent screen use has attracted increasing attention as a pivotal public-health concern. Prior studies have linked evening device use to delayed sleep onset [3, 7, 9, 12, 15]. It is worth noting that, importantly, the mechanisms remain unclear; light exposure, displaced sleep time, and arousal have each been proposed, but none has been isolated experimentally [4].

## Methods

We recruited 240 adolescents aged 13–17 from four schools between 2023 and 2024. Of the 240 participants, 130 identified as female and 120 identified as male. Sleep quality was measured with the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and screen time was self-reported. Participants were randomized to a two-week sleep-hygiene intervention (n = 118) or a waitlist control (n = 122).

## Results

Higher evening screen time was associated with worse sleep quality (r = 0.21, 95% CI 0.13 to 0.29), suggesting a possible link between screen exposure and sleep. The intervention did not significantly reduce PSQI scores relative to control (mean difference −0.6, 95% CI −1.3 to 0.1; p = 0.08). Our adaptive reminder system performed much better than the standard reminder schedule and was really robust.

One participant described the experience this way: "I'd put the phone down — then pick it right back up." We demonstrate that the adherence estimator is unbiased under random missingness (Theorem 1).

## Discussion

These findings demonstrate that screen time causes poor sleep in adolescents and pave the way for a new paradigm in digital-health policy. Additionally, the intervention showcases a seamless integration of behavioral science and technology. Because the sample was drawn from four schools in one region and screen time was self-reported, these results may not generalize to other populations.
